articles.title: Ollie, a privacy-focused AI assistant, is shutting down
articles.reason: 涵盖 AI product & news、Startup & business
articles.summary: As an increasing number of AI assistants flood the market, the founder of Ollie, an assistant that respected its users' privacy, says it will be shutting down in a week.
articles.full_text:
Ollie, a startup whose mission was to deliver an AI assistant that respected its users’ privacy, says that it will be shutting down in a week.

Bill Lennon, the company’s co-founder and CEO, took to X on Friday to deliver the news, noting that the app will officially shut down on November 6. “I’m really proud of what we accomplished,” Lennon said. “We built an incredible personal assistant with a small team, and learned a ton.

I’m grateful to our amazing team, our users, our investors, and everyone who supported us on this journey.” The text-based AI assistant market has exploded over the past year, as the increasingly powerful models that undergird such applications have made them significantly more useful for daily tasks.

Ollie, which discussed its $7.5 million seed round led by Khosla Ventures with TechCrunch in September, offered a subscription-based model.

The assistant was focused on helping families stay connected and organized.

The app connected to a user’s email and calendar, while also providing integrated functions to help with appointment bookings, meal planning, and bill payments.

The company had also planned to eventually move into household budgeting.

Crucially, Ollie was one of the first mainstream apps that managed to achieve SOC 2, a privacy compliance standard that companies can attain via an independent audit.

Unfortunately, user privacy has never been a hugely profitable aspect of the tech industry.

If anything, many new digital assistants present unique privacy challenges for their users — as companies like Instinct have shown .

Ultimately, the pressures of the burgeoning AI industry took a toll on the company, Lennon said. “We got close, but ultimately couldn’t keep up,” he added. “With Muse, Instinct, and others entering the space, it became harder to stand out, grow, and raise the capital we needed to succeed.” Ollie’s customers will receive instructions on how to export data and receive refunds in the coming days, Lennon added.

articles.title: Anthropic expected to receive high ‘junk’ rating from credit agencies following IPO, FT report says
articles.reason: 涵盖 AI product & news、Startup & business
articles.summary: Blackstone's forecast is just a prediction, but naturally, a high junk rating would make it more difficult and costlier for Anthropic to raise the money to keep funding its massive spending that has undergirded its business.
articles.full_text:
In Brief Posted: 2:52 PM PDT · October 30, 2026 Lucas Ropek Anthropic expected to receive high ‘junk’ rating from credit agencies following IPO, FT report says Anthropic is expected to receive a high “junk” rating from credit rating agencies following its initial public offering, according to a report from the Financial Times.

The FT says the investment giant Blackstone, the anchor investor in a recent $63 billion deal to finance Anthropic’s chips, told investors in the deal that it expects the AI lab to receive a “high” junk rating after its IPO.

Previously, the FT notes, Blackstone had said the opposite: that the Claude maker would receive an investment-grade rating (indicating low risk for lenders) before 2027 rolls around.

Now Blackstone expects double B range rating, the top tier of speculative “junk” grade, according to the reporting.

TechCrunch reached out to Anthropic and Blackstone but both declined to comment.

Blackstone’s forecast is just a prediction, but naturally, a high junk rating would make it more difficult and costlier for Anthropic to raise the money to keep funding its massive spending that has undergirded its business.

The lab has been on a spending spree, racking up large compute power deals throughout the past 12 months, which has worried investors .

Anthropic officially filed to go public earlier this week, kicking off a wave of speculation about how the massive IPO would impact the broader AI industry .

articles.full_text:
AI News Tech Sam Altman says it’s better for RAM to be in a data center than on your desk As OpenAI’s buying spree squeezes the world’s supply of RAM, its CEO explains why he needs so much.﻿ As OpenAI’s buying spree squeezes the world’s supply of RAM, its CEO explains why he needs so much.﻿ by Stevie Bonifield Oct 30, 2026, 8:48 PM UTC Link Share Gift Image: Justin Sullivan / Getty Images Part Of RAM price hikes: the latest on the global memory shortage see all updates Stevie Bonifield is a news writer covering all things consumer tech.

Stevie started out at Laptop Mag writing news and reviews on hardware, gaming, and AI.

Asked about supply chain shortages, like the ongoing RAM shortage , OpenAI CEO Sam Altman said in an interview that it’s “terrible” to have RAM in personal PCs instead of data centers.

During his appearance on the Cheeky Pint podcast, where he also commented on AI’s impact on math , Altman said: “A lot of people want local inference.

And somehow, they assume that the problem is solved now because we are going to have open-source models, we’re going to be able to run them on our computers, and so we’re not going to need all the stuff in the data center.

But from a global allocation perspective, actually, it’s quite terrible to have everybody have a bunch of the world’s limited supply of DRAM sitting in their own computer and being used five percent of the time.

You want maximum utilization in the cloud if you’re trying to deal with this very supply constrained environment.

And somehow everyone’s— many people’s intuition is the opposite of that.” Whether Altman meant your gaming PC or developers working with something like the Surface RTX Spark Dev Box or the new touchscreen MacBook Pro , the outcome is the same.

Right now, memory companies Samsung and SK Hynix have long term deals with cloud service operators and projects like OpenAI’s Stargate that have reserved much of the world’s RAM output over the next few years.

And the billions they’re willing to lay out for chips is why the laptops, phones, and other tech you use are getting more expensive right now.

articles.title: The biggest names in AI are backing a new way to opt out of scraping
articles.summary: OpenAI, Google, Microsoft, and Anthropic say they will adopt a new standard that publishers can use to opt out of being scraped by AI, as reported earlier by Search Engine Roundtable. With this control, publishers can apply their AI training preferences across multiple AI companies, instead of setting them individually. The shared "policy token" signal […]
articles.full_text:
Tech AI News The biggest names in AI are backing a new way to opt out of scraping The new control will allow publishers to apply their AI training preferences across multiple crawlers.

The new control will allow publishers to apply their AI training preferences across multiple crawlers. by Emma Roth Oct 30, 2026, 8:26 PM UTC Link Share Gift Illustration by Cath Virginia / The Verge | Photos from Getty Images Emma Roth is a news writer who covers the streaming wars, consumer tech, crypto, social media, and much more.

Previously, she was a writer and editor at MUO.

OpenAI, Google, Microsoft, and Anthropic say they will adopt a new standard that publishers can use to opt out of being scraped by AI, as reported earlier by Search Engine Roundtable .

With this control, publishers can apply their AI training preferences across multiple AI companies, instead of setting them individually.

The shared “policy token” signal is proposed by Kevin Kelley, a technical lead for standards at Anthropic, as part of the Internet Engineering Task Force (IETF).

It will live within a website’s robots.txt file , which has long signaled which web crawlers can and can’t scrape a site — whether for search indexing, archiving, or AI training.

Currently, sites have to signal their AI training preferences separately to each AI company.

The announcement comes as publishers grapple with the continuing influx of AI crawlers scraping their sites and feeding their content into AI models.

Some companies and organizations have attempted to combat unauthorized scraping, with the Really Simple Licensing (RSL) standard giving publishers the ability to charge crawlers that visit their sites, and Cloudflare blocking AI crawlers by default .

OpenAI , Google , Microsoft , and Anthropic say they will restrict their AI crawlers from accessing a site if they encounter the shared token.

Meta communications head Andy Stone also signaled support for the new setting, but doesn’t say whether the company will honor it. “We believe creating a common signal that conveys such preferences to multiple providers at once is an important step,” Stone says. “And we look forward to working with other AI companies on the standards and their implementation across the industry.” Microsoft says it will offer granular controls that will give publishers the ability to opt out of AI training or AI grounding , the process of pointing an AI model to a verified source of information to reduce hallucinations.

Microsoft notes that websites will still appear in Bing’s search results regardless of their preferences.

Google previously implemented similar controls that allow sites to control whether their content appears in AI search features or is used for AI training, without impacting visibility in search.

While Anthropic has already adopted the signal, Google and Microsoft plan to support it next year.

OpenAI says it will implement it in the “coming months.” Update, October 30th: Added a comment from Meta.

articles.title: Google’s first data center satellite is online and writing poetry
articles.summary: The first TPU in space is running a Google DeepMind Gemma 4 model and writing cheesy poetry.
articles.full_text:
Google Suncatcher’s prototype space data center is online and communicating with the ground after launching earlier this month alongside more than 100 other spacecraft on a SpaceX Falcon 9 rocket.

The satellite, which carries four Google Tensor Processing Units (TPUs) and generates up to 1 kW of electricity, is intended to pave the way for future networks of close-flying satellites performing large inference workloads in orbit.

However, the power demands of the TPU mean it can only turn one on for about 20 minutes at a time, complicating the already tricky business of space-to-ground communications.

After a commissioning process that tested out the satellite’s subsystems over about three weeks, the spacecraft was ready to work.

When engineers on the ground sent their first prompt this week, they asked the model pre-loaded onto the satellite, Google DeepMind’s Gemma 4, to write a haiku about being in space.

And thus: Blue marble below Data streams in silent grace Starlight feeds my core. ✨ Google said it tested the model with these space-themed limericks (they should have sent a poet?) and, perhaps more importantly, the company asked the spacecraft to report on the orbital conditions around the satellite.

A spokesperson told TechCrunch that the satellite was operating nominally.

The ongoing test campaign will examine how the chips perform under thermal stress and in the space radiation environment.

Google has extensively tested its TPUs in particle accelerators on Earth, but now needs to see how radiation’s real effects on their hardware in space affect their processor.

Radiation can cause “bit flips” — causing a stored value in computer memory — and that in turn can corrupt data without triggering typical monitoring tools.

Testing on the ground suggested the impact of radiation would be minimal for inference workloads and more of a problem for training a model, but now the Google team will get to assess those dynamics in reality, not a simulation.

If the TPUs onboard this spacecraft prove capable, the next step will be launching two more satellites equipped with the advanced chips in 2027.

Those spacecraft will support higher power generation and demonstrate inter-satellite optical links.

Google’s Suncatcher project is largely alone among visions for space-based data centers in planning on high-speed links between the satellites to support coherent distributed workloads; SpaceX’s data centers are also expected to use laser links but also to orbit too far apart to share processing effectively.

Companies like Starcloud and Cowboy Space expect to perform inference loads on individual satellites.

Google and SpaceX’s visions are closely linked.

Alphabet, Google’s parent company, holds a significant investment stake in SpaceX.

And to launch their orbital data centers, both companies will require Starship, the still-in-development heavy-lift rocket at the center of Elon Musk’s space vision, to be fully and rapidly reusable.

In a peer-reviewed analysis published earlier this month, Suncatcher researchers estimated that SpaceX would need to fly Starship 1,800 times to achieve the same learning-driven cost reductions it saw with its earlier vehicles.

Suncatcher is a classic Google moonshot — the company’s focus is on designing infrastructure that will be economical in the 2030s.

Getting there, however, may depend on how the rest of the company responds to the pressures and opportunities of AI in the near term.

Alphabet, Google’s parent company, saw its stock plunge this week after reporting that efforts to insert AI into its search businesses are hurting ad revenue growth.

Correction: The Suncatcher prototype satellite has four TPUs onboard, but can only operate one at a time.
